title: Biscuit and Clover's Bell Adventure
markdown:
On Farmer Giles’s sunny farm, Biscuit the puppy was a whirlwind of fluff and wiggles. Floppy ears. A tail that could knock a teacup over if a teacup was unwise enough to sit near. He chased butterflies, sniffed interesting smells, and pounced on dandelions until they puffed. Clover the calf was as sweet and steady as a summer afternoon. Her eyes were melted caramel. When she chewed her cud she looked as if she were thinking the world’s biggest thoughts. They napped side by side in the warm grass, Biscuit’s paws still twitching with leftover chases.

One bright morning a peculiar sound drifted over the meadow.

Ting-a-ling.

It was silvery, like tiny stars that had forgotten it was daytime. Biscuit’s ears turned like furry dishes.

“What’s that, Clover?”

Clover chewed, blinked. “Different. Not cows. Not chickens. It makes my ears want to dance.”

“A happy secret,” Biscuit yipped. “Let’s find the most wonderful farmyard sound.” He bounced. Then his ears drooped. The wish felt too big for his fluffy chest. He remembered a hard wind, a shutter bang, legs gone wobbly. Silence before a bang made his tail tuck.

“What if it’s too far?” he whispered. “What if it’s too loud? I’m not good at brave when things get wiggly. Silence makes my tail tuck.” His tail tucked a hair. He nearly turned toward the barn.

Clover nudged him with a soft nose, warm as a patch of sun. “We’ll go together. You have me. I have you. Farmer Giles calls us when the clouds go pink. We’ll be back.”

The sun was already high. The sound might fade. Biscuit gave a determined little bark that surprised even him, and hopped the low pasture fence. Clover leapt after, long legs easy. Tall grass tickled their bellies. Flowers stood in sunshine-yellow and sky-blue. The ting-a-ling was clearer, a sweet whisper leading them on.

The meadow was a whole new world. Grass taller than Biscuit’s ears swayed and tickled. A beetle hiked a blade and paid them no mind. The ting-a-ling drifted, then hid behind a hedge, then came back, as if it liked being followed.

A babbling brook crossed their way. The only bridge was a log, smooth and curved like a sleeping giant, and it looked wiggly. Water talked to the stones underneath, cheerful and unhelpful.

Biscuit’s tail stopped. Ears flat. “I don’t like wiggly. My tummy might flip.”

He almost turned back. His heart thumped a worried rhythm. Then he heard Clover’s breathing, steady as cud-chewing, right behind him.

“You can do it,” she mooed, voice like a warm hug. “One paw after another. See that bright red poppy on the other side?”

Biscuit puffed his chest. He looked at the poppy. One step. The log made a tiny traitorous roll. Another step. He wobbled. His paws slipped on the wood. He did not fall. He kept his eyes on Clover, and on the red. Halfway, he wanted to sit down and become a very small statue. He did not sit. He hopped off and shook himself hard. Droplets sparkled. A tiny bit of bounce came back. His tail tried a wag.

They pushed next through buttercups that tickled noses and ears with velvety petals. They giggled. They wriggled. The sweet grassy scent filled everything. Biscuit tumbled, sneezed a yellow puff, and for a moment forgot the bell because tumbling was so good. Clover waited, caramel eyes kind, until he remembered.

“Onwards,” he barked, shaking a petal from his ear.

Then the sound was right ahead. They pushed through the last buttercups and found a tiny bluebird on a tall daisy, wings tucked, eyes worried. On its leg, tied with a daisy chain, hung a miniature sparkling bell.

Ting-a-ling.

Beautiful. And stuck. The chain dangled and tugged. The bird could not fly properly. It chirped a thin worried note at the sky.

“Oh, the poor thing,” Clover whispered.

Biscuit understood trapped. He wanted to help. A bright yellow butterfly danced nearby. His legs itched to chase. Helping meant staying still. Being careful. Not chasing. He imagined his own paw catching in something unexpected, and the itch went quieter.

“We have to get it free,” he said, surprisingly firm.

Clover lowered her head, eyes on the chain. Biscuit held still. For a puppy who loved to wiggle, still was a mountain. His tail twitched. The butterfly looped, yellow as butter, almost close enough to pounce. Biscuit’s paws prickled. He could almost feel the joy of a good run. He kept his eyes on the bluebird’s bright worried gaze instead. He felt the tickly daisy petals on his nose, heard leaves rustle, smelled meadow perfume. He became a small fluffy statue of helpfulness. Clover used her wet nose to loosen the knot, slow and precise, as if the daisy chain were a riddle that disliked being rushed.

Pop. The daisy chain fell away into the grass, just another flower among flowers.

The bluebird chirped delight, hopped, spread its wings, and flew up. The bell rang a cheerful ting-a-ling now, full of air. The bird circled, looped as if showing a path, seemed to wink, and soared. The butterfly, ignored, went on dancing anyway, which was a kind of happy ending too.

The sky turned rosy, peach and lavender on the clouds. Biscuit and Clover followed the silvery song home. Tall grass brushed them like a welcome. They crossed the wiggly log — Biscuit remembered his paws this time, poppy to poppy in his mind — and hopped the fence. Farmer Giles was just coming out to call them for supper, voice as ordinary and safe as a bucket.

In their field the evening went soft. Usually Biscuit grew antsy in quiet, hunting a new noise, nudging Clover for a romp. Tonight he sat beside her. His tail thumped a slow happy rhythm. An owl hooted far off. Wind whispered in the trees. Friends munched a peaceful chorus. Farmer Giles’s bucket clinked once at the gate, then the farm remembered how to be still.

He looked at Clover with a proud stretch of grin. He had stayed still when staying still was the brave thing. The butterfly could dance without him. The bell’s song went on somewhere above the barn, small and free, and Biscuit’s tail did not tuck at the quiet. It kept time, thump, thump, like a tiny farmyard bell of his own.
